newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Russia has sold no missiles to Iran.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Russia has sold no missiles to Iran.

text.p: The U.S. State Department, citing intelligence and other information, said on Wednesday it did not believe that Russia had sold advanced anti-aircraft missiles to Iran.
But spokesman Nicholas Burns said he did not know whether Moscow had discussed with Iran the sale of such missiles, as reported on Wednesday by the Washington Times newspaper.

Quoting Pentagon officials, The Washington Times said that in talks in February Russian arms dealers offered Iranian intelligence agents several types of missiles including up to 500 "Igla" shoulder-launched models. It said Tehran planned to supply some of these to anti-Israeli Hizbollah guerrillas in Lebanon.
Such a sale would violate a 1994 pledge to the United States by Russian President Boris Yeltsin not to engage in new weapons sales to Iran.

"Based on our conversations with the Russian government at the very highest level, based on all the intelligence information available to us ... the United States does not believe that Russia has transferred to Iran advanced missiles," Burns said.

But, asked at a briefing whether the two countries might have discussed a sale, he said: "You're asking me to prove almost the impossible ... I cannot confirm that. But I don't think I'm in a position to say, no, Russians and Iranians have never discussed it."

The Washington Times said that in addition to the Iglas, the Russians also offered Iran SA-10 and SA-12 missiles. These would be delivered within a year of signing a contract, Pentagon officials were quoted as saying.

Burns admitted that any sales of SA-10s or SA-12s, "would provide Iran with dangerous new capabilities and would certainly violate" Yeltsin's pledge, which was later codified in a 1995 U.S.-Russian agreement.
He said the United States would continue to discuss the issue of sales to Iran with the Russian government.

Yeltsin promised during a 1994 summit with President Bill Clinton in Washington that Russia would not enter into new arms contracts with Iran, and would close out existing contracts within a few years.
The existing contracts did not involve any new weapon systems, the Russians said.
